text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
- Former TV journalist Michael Born convicted of fraud for selling faked TV documentaries to German networks.
- President Roman Herzog calls for more tolerance and humanity, urges Germans to become better neighbours.
- German parliament members want to meet Iraq leader Saddam Hussein during trip to meet government leaders in January.
- Chambers of Industry and Trade leader Hans Peter Stihl calls for new round of "Alliance for Jobs" among government labour and industry.
- German industry launches massive criticism at government's plans to raise value-added tax and other taxes. Fears also growing that planned tax reform for 1999 will fail.
- Deutsche Telekom will have special low tarifs during holiday in bid to get customers to make more calls.
- Moody's sinks Deutsche Bank's ratings on long-term deposits from A to B+.
- Eastern German economy looks for better days, economic barometers points for improvement in months ahead.
- Interior Minister Manfred Kanther wants to use private firms to improve government efficiency in such areas as accounting and payrolls.

- SPD says debt reaches record levels in 1996. At the end of November the federal government had a shortfall of 92.8 billion marks, that was already far above the budget plan for the full year of 59.9 billion marks.
- Greens party loses further politicians in east Germany. Former state parliament member Christine Grabe said she was quitting the party.
